item.title: Health insurance for Swiss abroad: obligations
item.description: Learn the rules for health insurance of Swiss retirees and workers abroad: obligations, deadlines and a fixed deductible of 300 CHF.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Anyone receiving an AVS/AI pension is required to choose a basic health insurance within 3 months.
- The basic insurance can be Swiss or from the country of residence in the agreed EU/EFTA states.
- Only funds with more than 500,000 insured persons may cover those who leave Switzerland for the EU.

- **What**: insurance obligation for AVS/AI recipients abroad.
- When: decision within the first 3 months of residence (except Spain).
- Where: EU/EFTA countries (including the United Kingdom) and non‑EU countries.
- Who: Swiss retirees, posted workers, citizens without Swiss income.
- Amount: fixed deductible of 300 CHF for Swiss funds that cover abroad.
- Regulation: Federal Law on Health Insurance (LAMal).
- Authorities: AVS compensation funds, Organization of Swiss Abroad (OSE), Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA).

On 22 April 2025 Swissinfo published an article outlining the health‑insurance rules for Swiss citizens moving abroad. The analysis starts with the fundamental distinction between retirees and non‑retirees. Anyone receiving an AVS or AI pension from Switzerland is, in principle, obliged to take out basic health insurance under LAMal. However, Switzerland has negotiated optional rights with several countries, including all neighbours and Spain. In these states the retiree can decide whether to keep Swiss coverage or join the local scheme. The decision must be made within the first three months after the change of residence, with the exception of Spain where it can be postponed.

The article emphasizes that Swiss coverage is reserved for funds with more than 500,000 insured persons. Only these are authorised to guarantee coverage for people moving to an EU country. In addition, the deductible is set at 300 CHF, regardless of the country of residence. Premiums, as in Switzerland, vary canton by canton, but abroad they depend on the average claim cost in the host country; for example, a Visana policy in Poland costs almost five times as much as a CSS policy.

For citizens who do not receive an AVS/AI pension the situation changes. If a Swiss citizen moves to London for work, they must take out the mandatory basic insurance in the United Kingdom, because the place of work is the determining criterion. If they move to London without working and without receiving a Swiss pension, they can remain insured by a Swiss health fund. This possibility is not provided for by LAMal but by the Federal Insurance Contract Act (LCA). Funds may freely decide whether to accept, reserve, or reject the coverage.

These provisions have concrete impacts on emigration planning: retirees must assess within three months which coverage – Swiss or local – is more advantageous, taking into account the fixed deductible and the differentiated premiums. Workers on assignment or posted have a temporary Swiss coverage, usually for two years, extendable up to six years at the decision of the AVS funds. The article invites readers to consult the FDFA website for official information and the OSE for advisory services.

> "Anyone receiving a Swiss AVS pension must decide within three months where to take out basic insurance" (Swissinfo, 22 Apr 2025).

To explore premium differences between funds, you can use the insurance comparator. ### Implications for Swiss pensioners who emigrate
The rules outlined in this article introduce a series of practical choices for pensioners. First and foremost, the requirement to decide within three months means a precise timeline for financial planning. The fixed deductible of 300 CHF is an extra expense compared to the Swiss cantonal model, where the deductible may vary. This can affect the calculation of the net cost of coverage, especially for those with frequent medical expenses.

Another key factor is the difference in premiums between insurance funds. Funds with more than 500,000 insured persons, such as CSS or Visana, offer lower rates thanks to a broader risk pool. However, the case of Poland shows that premiums can vary dramatically (Visana is nearly five times more expensive than CSS). For those moving to countries with high healthcare costs, the option agreement may be more advantageous if the country offers lower premiums or a smaller deductible.

From the perspective of the federal system, the possibility to choose the country of insurance strengthens pensioners' freedom of movement, but requires coordination between Swiss authorities (AVS funds, FDFA) and the health authorities of the host countries. LAMal remains the reference legal framework, but exceptions (e.g. Spain) show only limited flexibility.

### Workers without AVS/AI pension
For workers who do not receive a pension, the rule is more complex. If the workplace is abroad, the host country's regulations require local insurance. This means that a Swiss citizen employed in London must register with the NHS (National Health Service) or a private British insurance, depending on UK requirements. The difference compared to LAMal is that the federal law on insurance contracts (LCA) allows Swiss funds to offer coverage voluntarily, but it is not mandatory.

This flexibility creates scenarios of potential double coverage: a worker can keep the Swiss fund as a backup, but must still pay the host country's premiums. The decision depends on the cost-benefit ratio, the duration of the assignment, and the presence of any bilateral agreements between Switzerland and the country of employment.

### Comparison before/after current regulations
Before the EU/EFTA option was defined, many pensioners had to automatically keep Swiss coverage, even if living in countries with higher healthcare costs. The current right of option allows you to choose the most economical solution, but introduces the three-month deadline and fixed deductible. For workers, the distinction between secondment (Swiss coverage for a maximum of two to six years) and permanent relocation (local obligation) remains unchanged, but the possibility of a backup via LCA adds an extra choice.

### Impact on the cantons
Cantons no longer have a direct role in choosing insurance for residents abroad, but the difference in premiums remains influenced by the canton of origin, since funds calculate premiums based on the average cost of claims of their insured, which depends on the canton of provenance. This can create disparities between insured persons from cantons with higher premiums (e.g. Zurich) and those from less expensive cantons (e.g. Ticino). Pensioners should also consider this aspect when deciding their coverage.

To check how premiums affect your situation, you can use our [health insurance calculator](nav:health).


## Useful planning tools
To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step‑by‑step guide to choosing basic health insurance abroad
1. **Check your pension**: make sure you receive an AVS or AI pension from Switzerland. If yes, you are subject to the LAMal obligation.
2. Identify your country of residence: verify whether the country is on the EU/EFTA list with the right of option (including neighboring countries and Spain). The list is available on the DFAE website.
3. Three‑month deadline: mark the start date of residence on your calendar and count three months to make a decision. Only for Spain can the deadline be postponed.
4. Compare insurers: see which Swiss insurers have more than 500,000 insured persons (e.g., CSS, Visana). Check the premiums specific to the country of residence; the deductible will still be 300 CHF.
5. Request quotes: contact the selected insurers and ask for a quote that includes annual premium, deductible and geographic coverage.
6. Evaluate the local option: obtain information on premiums and deductibles of the local health‑care system. Compare them with the Swiss quote.
7. Decide and subscribe: within the three months, inform the Swiss insurer of your choice or subscribe to the local insurance. Keep the confirmation for possible tax checks.
8. Update AVS: notify AVS of the new coverage status to avoid penalties.

### Emergency scenarios
- If the decision is postponed (Spain only), you can keep Swiss coverage for up to 12 months, but you should check the specific conditions with the insurer.
- If you miss the deadline: the Swiss insurer may consider the coverage terminated and impose penalties or request a refund of premiums not owed.
- If you move to another country again: you must repeat the procedure within three months of the new move.

### Useful tools
- [Health insurance calculator](nav:health) to compare premiums and deductibles.
- DFAE website for the list of countries with the right of option.
- Organization of Swiss Abroad (OSE) for personalized advice.

💡 Practical tip: keep a digital folder with all insurance documents (contracts, confirmations, AVS communications); it makes interactions with insurers and authorities much easier.

🔗 To learn more about the cost of living in relation to insurance premiums, visit our [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) section.

item.title: La finanza svizzera sotto esame per il clima
item.description: La Svizzera è una potenza finanziaria, ma il suo settore finanziario continua a investire miliardi in progetti legati ai combustibili fossili.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - La Svizzera è una potenza finanziaria con un settore finanziario che gestisce circa 9'200 miliardi di franchi di patrimoni. - Il settore finanziario svizzero continua a investire miliardi in progetti legati ai combustibili fossili. - Una nuova iniziativa popolare chiede norme ambientali più severe in materia di investimenti. ## Fatti chiave - **Cosa**: Il settore finanziario svizzero investe miliardi in progetti legati ai combustibili fossili. - Quando: La Svizzera è una potenza finanziaria dal 2024. - Dove: Il settore finanziario svizzero è presente in tutto il mondo. - Chi: Le banche, le compagnie assicurative e i fondi pensione svizzeri sono coinvolti. - Importo: I prestiti e gli investimenti azionari finanziati dalla Svizzera nei settori ad alta intensità di carbonio generano tra i 700 e i 900 milioni di tonnellate di CO₂ equivalente all'anno. La Svizzera è una potenza finanziaria con un settore finanziario che gestisce circa 9'200 miliardi di franchi di patrimoni. Tuttavia, il settore finanziario svizzero continua a investire miliardi in progetti legati ai combustibili fossili, che generano fino a 18 volte più emissioni rispetto a quelle interne dell'intera Svizzera. Questo contrasta con gli impegni globali di ridurre le emissioni di gas serra e raggiungere gli obiettivi del Paris Agreement. ### Investimenti Fossili in Svizzera Il cantone di Zurigo, noto per la sua finanza globale, è un esempio significativo di questa tendenza. Secondo un rapporto dell'Università di Zurigo, i fondi pensione del cantone investono circa 1,5 miliardi di franchi in progetti di carbone e petrolio ogni anno. Questo rappresenta oltre il 5% dei loro investimenti totali, e le emissioni generate da questi investimenti equivalgono a quelle di circa 1,2 milioni di automobili all'anno. ### Iniziative Popolari Una nuova iniziativa popolare, denominata 'Finanza per il Clima', è stata avviata in alcuni cantoni svizzeri. Questa iniziativa richiede che le banche e le compagnie assicurative svizzere adottino standard più severi per gli investimenti in settori ad alta intensità di carbonio. L'iniziativa è stata presentata in cantoni come Vaud e Ticino, dove le discussioni sono in corso per determinare la portata e l'impatto delle future normative. ### Normative e Regolamentazioni La Svizzera ha già adottato alcune normative per ridurre l'impatto ambientale del settore finanziario. Ad esempio, la legge sulla sostenibilità finanziaria, entrata in vigore nel 2021, obbliga le banche svizzere a valutare l'impatto ambientale dei loro investimenti e a comunicare pubblicamente sui loro progressi. Tuttavia, queste normative sono spesso considerate insufficienti per affrontare la sfida climatica. ### Checklist Operativa Per affrontare questa sfida, il settore finanziario svizzero potrebbe seguire una checklist operativa: 1. Valutazione Ambientale: Implementare strumenti di valutazione ambientale per tutti gli investimenti. 2. Divestimento: Considerare il divestimento da settori ad alta intensità di carbonio. 3. Transparenza: Aumentare la trasparenza sulle emissioni generate dagli investimenti. 4. Collaborazione: Collaborare con altre istituzioni finanziarie per sviluppare soluzioni comuni. ### Confronto tra Scenari Un confronto tra due scenari pratici illumina l'importanza di queste azioni: - Scenario 1: Continua con gli investimenti attuali. Le emissioni di CO₂ equivalenti aumenteranno, rendendo difficile raggiungere gli obiettivi del Paris Agreement. - Scenario 2: Adozione di standard più severi e divestimento dai settori ad alta intensità di carbonio. Le emissioni potrebbero essere ridotte del 30-40%, contribuendo significativamente agli obiettivi di riduzione delle emissioni. ### Esempi Concreti La banca UBS, una delle più grandi banche svizzere, ha recentemente annunciato un piano per ridurre del 50% le emissioni generate dai suoi investimenti entro il 2030. Questo piano include l'aumento dell'investimento in energia rinnovabile e la riduzione degli investimenti in carbone. Tuttavia, molti osservatori ritengono che questi sforzi siano ancora insufficienti per affrontare la crisi climatica. ### Conclusione La Svizzera, con il suo settore finanziario potente, ha un ruolo cruciale da giocare nella transizione verso un'economia a bassa emissione. Tuttavia, la sfida è grande e richiede azioni immediate e decisive. Le iniziative popolari e le normative esistenti rappresentano un primo passo, ma è necessario fare di più per garantire che il settore finanziario svizzero contribuisca positivamente alla lotta contro il cambiamento climatico. ## The Environmental Impact of the Swiss Financial Sector

The Swiss financial sector has a significant environmental impact, primarily due to its investments in fossil fuel-related projects. According to a 2022 McKinsey study, loans and equity investments financed by Switzerland in carbon-intensive sectors generate between 700 and 900 million tons of CO₂ equivalent annually. This figure does not include government bonds and capital market operations, suggesting the actual total could be higher.

For instance, the Canton of Ticino, known for its chemical and petrochemical industry, is one of the major contributors to these emissions. According to a 2021 report by the Ticinese Environmental Agency, the chemical sector in Ticino is responsible for approximately 40% of the region's CO₂ emissions, with many companies operating in carbon-intensive industries. Swiss banks, including UBS and Credit Suisse, have financed numerous projects in this sector, indirectly contributing to CO₂ emissions.

## Stricter Environmental Regulations for Investments

A new popular initiative, titled 'For a Sustainable Financial Center,' has been launched by several environmental and civil society organizations, including WWF and Greenpeace. The initiative calls for Swiss banks, insurance companies, and pension funds to be required to do more for the climate and nature, making the sector truly sustainable.

> 'Our goal is to compel financial institutions to adopt more sustainable practices and stop financing projects that harm our planet,' stated a Greenpeace representative.

The initiative proposes a series of concrete measures, including:

- **Ban on financing carbon-intensive projects**: Banks and pension funds should be required not to finance projects generating more than 100 tons of CO₂ equivalent per year.
- Emission reduction targets: Financial institutions should be required to set emission reduction targets and monitor progress.
- Transparency and reporting: Banks and pension funds should be required to publicly report on their environmental practices and investments.

📊 Key Data:
- According to a 2020 Swiss Re report, CO₂ emissions linked to damage caused by storms and floods in Switzerland have increased by 50% in the last 20 years.
- Another 2019 study by Credit Suisse revealed that the Swiss financial and insurance sectors are responsible for 10% of global CO₂ emissions.

💡 Operational Checklist:
1. Evaluate current investments and identify carbon-intensive ones.
2. Set emission reduction targets and plan necessary actions.
3. Implement transparency and reporting policies.
4. Regularly monitor and update environmental practices.

⚠️ Challenges and Considerations:
- The transition to a more sustainable financial sector will require time and resources.
- Resistance from large banks and pension funds could be a significant obstacle.
- Cooperation between the public and private sectors will be crucial for the initiative's success.

In conclusion, while the Swiss financial sector plays a significant role in financing carbon-intensive projects, there are promising signs of change. The 'For a Sustainable Financial Center' initiative represents an important step toward more sustainable and responsible finance.

item.title: Switzerland rejects US tariffs on forced labor, talks underway
item.description: Bern rejects US accusations and negotiates in Paris. 12.5% tariffs under discussion, comment deadline July 6, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief

- US tariffs of 12.5% against Switzerland over alleged forced labour
- Parmelin meets Greer on sidelines of OECD conference in Paris
- Bern vehemently rejects American accusations
- White House deadline for comments: 6 July 2026

## Key facts

- **What**: US accusations over insufficient forced labour enforcement, proposed 12.5% tariffs
- When: Meeting today in Paris; current tariffs until 24 July 2026
- Where: Paris, OECD ministerial conference
- Who: Guy Parmelin (Swiss president, economy minister), Jamieson Greer (US trade representative)
- Amount: Additional 12.5% tariffs proposed by the United States
- Institution: Federal Department of Economic Affairs (FDEA), OECD
- Deadline: 6 July 2026 for comments to the White House

### The diplomatic confrontation in Paris

Guy Parmelin, 66-year-old president of the Confederation and minister of economic affairs, restated the Swiss position today in Paris during a bilateral meeting with Jamieson Greer, the American trade representative. The appointment took place on the margins of the OECD ministerial conference, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, bringing together two key figures from their respective executives at a moment of trade tension.

The Federal Department of Economic Affairs (FDEA), led by Parmelin himself, took a stand with a sharpness rare in Swiss diplomatic vocabulary. Bern rejects the American accusations "vehemently", contesting the premise that Switzerland does not do enough to prevent the importation of products made with forced labour. The Swiss response rests on three pillars: state regulation, mandatory risk assessments initiated by the private sector, and international cooperation. These approaches, the FDEA explains to Keystone-ATS, "differ in method, but not in objective and effectiveness". The closing statement in the press release is equally peremptory: "American industry is not harmed by Swiss practice".

Parmelin announced through his own social channels that "both parties will continue to work on solutions", a formulation that leaves the door open to negotiation without yielding on the substance of the accusations. The tone is one of firmness without rupture, typical of Swiss diplomacy when dossiers touch strategic economic interests.

### The tariff procedure and timelines in play

The FDEA clarified one relevant operational detail: the recommended tariffs will not enter into force immediately. They should instead replace the current ones, whose expiry is set for 24 July 2026. This timeframe offers a space for negotiation that both parties appear intent on exploiting. Talks for a trade agreement with the United States continue, taking into account the latest developments that emerged from the American report. The Swiss government is examining the document in depth and will discuss options for action, while the White House expects formal comments by 6 July.

Switzerland thus finds itself in a position not entirely dissimilar from other European countries subject to the same American investigation, but with a specific aggravating factor: the weight of precision, pharmaceutical and watchmaking exports to the United States market. Every percentage point of additional tariff translates into measurable revenue contractions for the companies that employ thousands of workers between Zurich, Basel, Geneva and the industrial heart of the country. ### Why forced labour has become a commercial weapon

The United States has turned the fight against forced labour into a tool of aggressive trade policy, with direct effects on Swiss companies that export overseas. The American law known as the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, later extended to broader contexts, requires customs authorities to presume forced labour is widespread in specific regions or sectors, placing the burden of proof on importing firms. Switzerland, while sharing the goal, applies a different approach: risk assessments based on evidence, shared responsibility between public and private actors, and no presumption of geographic guilt.

For Swiss businesses, this methodological divergence translates into a dual operational challenge. On the one hand they must demonstrate the cleanliness of their supply chains according to American standards that do not match Swiss ones; on the other hand they risk trade sanctions based on a political assessment of their control system. The DFE, in its response, highlighted exactly this: the effectiveness is equivalent, only the path differs. It is an argument that resists tweet‑size simplification but requires lengthy, specialised technical negotiations.

### The impact on cantons and the national economy

The repercussions of a 12.5% tariff increase would not be distributed evenly across Swiss territory. Cantons with higher export intensity to the USA — Basel‑City (pharmaceuticals), Geneva (luxury watchmaking, commodities), Zurich (precision machinery, technology), Ticino (components, fashion) — would face immediate competitive pressure. SMEs, which make up the fabric of the Swiss production system, have lower margins than pharmaceutical giants and could be forced to cut orders or reorganise supply chains already strained by years of geopolitical uncertainty.

The cost of living in Switzerland, already among the highest in the world, risks an additional indirect burden. If US exports contract, pressure on real wages rises, especially in sectors where foreign demand underpins salary levels. The wage‑to‑purchasing‑power ratio, already closely monitored by those working in Switzerland, could take a negative turn in areas dependent on trans‑Atlantic export. It is no coincidence that the DFE chose to respond with maximum visibility: the entire Alpine arc, from the Jura to the Gotthard, has stakes in play.

item.description: The Geneva University Hospital identified the hantavirus strain responsible for an epidemic outbreak on a cruise ship in May 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- The Geneva University Hospital has identified the hantavirus strain responsible for an epidemic outbreak on a cruise ship in May 2026.
- The Andes strain is the only hantavirus known to be transmitted from human to human.
- Identifying the viral species is crucial for understanding its transmission dynamics, severity, and origin.

## Key facts
- **What**: Identification of the hantavirus strain responsible for an epidemic outbreak.
- When: May 2026.
- Where: Geneva University Hospital (HUG).
- Who: Francisco-Javier Perez Rodriguez, biologist heading the emerging viruses section of the laboratory.
- Amount: Not specified.

On May 4, 2026, an infected Swiss citizen was admitted to the University Hospital of Zurich (USZ). Here, blood samples, urine samples, and respiratory samples were taken using swabs similar to those used for Covid-19 tests. The samples were then sealed inside three distinct protective layers for transport, as per the protocol for handling viral pathogens.

On the same day, the specimens were transported by car to the National Reference Center for Emerging Viral Infections (CRIVE) in Geneva, which is part of the HUG virology laboratory network. Established in 2005, the center operates under a mandate and is partially funded by the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) with the aim of diagnosing emerging viruses such as dengue, SARS, or Zika.

### The identification process
CRIVE is one of the four Swiss laboratories certified for the highest level of biological containment. The facility is equipped with pressure-sealed doors and impermeable walls; furthermore, the water supply and ventilation systems are entirely independent from the rest of the hospital complex and undergo repeated decontamination cycles, both before and after each use.

The refrigerated samples containing the virus were opened inside biosafety cabinets: these are workstations equipped with special hoods designed to protect operators from contaminated air particles.

Using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), the same technique used for Covid, expert personnel extracted the viral genome from the sample. This procedure allowed the identification of the Andes strain, the only hantavirus known to be transmitted from human to human, although it requires close contact.

### Implications for public health
Identifying the viral species is crucial for understanding its transmission dynamics, severity, and origin. This discovery has provided the World Health Organization (WHO) with the necessary tools to better understand the mechanisms of the virus and to adopt the most appropriate measures to contain the outbreak.

The Andes strain can trigger hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, a severe and potentially lethal disease that impairs respiratory function. Since May 2, the day the WHO was alerted, a total of 11 cases, including three deaths, have been reported among the passengers of the MV Hondius ship. ## Practical analysis
The identification of the hantavirus strain by the Geneva University Hospitals has important implications for cross-border workers who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy. The ability to quickly and accurately diagnose emerging viruses is crucial for public health, especially in a cross-border context where people's mobility is high.

### Impact on cross-border workers
Cross-border workers who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy could be exposed to similar risks as Swiss residents. Although the Andes strain transmission from person to person requires close contact, it highlights the importance of rigorous hygiene measures and safety protocols in the workplace.

### Prevention measures
Companies employing cross-border workers should consider implementing additional safety protocols, such as regular sanitization of work environments and promoting hygiene practices among employees. Additionally, it is essential that cross-border workers are informed about the symptoms of hantavirus and the measures to take in case of suspected infection.

### Cross-border collaboration
Collaboration between Swiss and Italian health authorities is essential to effectively manage any hantavirus outbreaks. Sharing information and coordinating containment measures can help prevent the spread of the virus among cross-border workers and their residential communities.

### Implications for the healthcare system
The identification of the hantavirus strain by the HUG demonstrates the importance of investing in high-security laboratories and specialized personnel. For cross-border workers, this means having access to faster and more accurate diagnoses, which can make a difference in managing any infections.

### Economic considerations
The management of emerging virus outbreaks can have a significant economic impact, especially for cross-border workers who depend on work in Switzerland. The temporary closure of workplaces or reduced productivity due to illness can affect the incomes of cross-border workers and their families.

### Future prospects
The discovery of the hantavirus strain by the HUG paves the way for further research and the development of more effective treatments. For cross-border workers, this could mean greater safety in the workplace and better protection against infectious diseases.

If you are a cross-border worker and suspect you have been exposed to hantavirus, it is important to act quickly and follow the appropriate procedures to protect your health and that of others.

### Step-by-step procedure
1. **Recognize the symptoms**: Symptoms of hantavirus may include fever, muscle aches, fatigue, and difficulty breathing. If you experience these symptoms, consult a doctor immediately.

2. Contact your doctor: Inform your doctor about your symptoms and the possibility of exposure to hantavirus. It is important to provide detailed information about your recent history, including any travel or contact with infected individuals.

3. Isolation: If you suspect you are infected, avoid close contact with other people to prevent transmission of the virus. Follow your doctor's instructions for isolation.

4. Diagnostic tests: Your doctor may recommend diagnostic tests to confirm the infection. These tests may include blood tests and respiratory samples.

5. Treatment: There is no specific treatment for hantavirus, but managing symptoms and medical support can improve the chances of recovery. Follow your doctor's instructions carefully.

### Prevention
Prevention is key to avoiding hantavirus infection. Follow these measures to reduce the risk:

- Personal hygiene: Wash your hands regularly with water and soap, especially after touching potentially contaminated surfaces.

- Cleaning environments: Keep work and home environments clean and sanitized, especially if there are signs of rodent presence.

- Personal protection: Use personal protective equipment, such as masks and gloves, if you work in environments at risk of exposure to rodents or their droppings.

### Conclusion
The identification of the hantavirus strain by the University Hospital of Geneva is an important step in the management of infectious diseases. For cross-border workers, this means having access to faster and more accurate diagnoses, which can make a difference in managing any infections. Follow prevention measures and consult a doctor immediately if you experience suspicious symptoms.

## In brief
- Cross-border workers in the EU/EFTA enjoy freedom of movement, with visas required outside Europe
- Platforms such as LinkedIn Jobs and Eures are essential for job searches
- Soliswiss and embassies provide consultations on permits and regulations
- Rules regarding dismissals and contracts vary by country

**Cosa**: Guide to finding work abroad for Swiss citizens
When: Information updated to 20/24 (source SWI swissinfo.ch)
Where: EU/EFTA countries and countries outside the EU (USA, Canada, Australia, Argentina)
Who: Swiss citizens, Ticino cross-border workers, Soliswiss and Airswift consultants
Amount: Not specified yet (costs for visas and permits vary by country)

Working abroad is an increasingly considered option for Ticino cross-border workers, especially in the dynamic Swiss labor market. According to SWI swissinfo.ch, Swiss citizens wishing to move across the border must first obtain information on the necessary permits for residency and work. In EU and EFTA countries, cross-border workers benefit from the freedom of movement of people, which allows them to reside and work without the need for special visas. This regulation is particularly relevant for those already working in Switzerland who wish to explore job opportunities in countries such as Italy, Germany, or France without having to deal with complex bureaucratic procedures.

For extra-EU countries like the United States, Canada, Australia, or Argentina, the situation differs. In these cases, special work visas or permits are required, and procedures can vary significantly. It is essential to contact the embassy or consulate of the country of interest directly to obtain accurate information on entry and stay regulations. For instance, embassies of the USA, Canada, Argentina, and Australia provide up-to-date details on the requirements necessary to obtain a work permit. The cooperative company Soliswiss, which offers consultations in English, French, and German, can be an excellent point of reference to clarify practical aspects related to emigration and work abroad.

### Analysis of the labor market: profile and opportunities

Before embarking on the search for work abroad, it is crucial to analyze your professional profile and the opportunities available in the destination country's labor market. Nicole Töpperwien, administrative director of Soliswiss, emphasizes that often the simplest way to secure employment is through direct contacts. Building a network on social media, such as LinkedIn, or becoming a member of professional associations in the country of interest can ease access to job opportunities. Julia Meir Lawi, Branch Director Geneva at Robert Half Schweiz, confirms that having the right contacts can open many doors, particularly in unfamiliar markets.

Another vital aspect is evaluating working conditions and the cost of living in the destination country. For example, rules on unfair dismissal protections and notice periods vary from country to country. Colby Clark of Airswift, a multinational recruitment company, warns that these differences can significantly affect job stability. It is therefore important to gather all information in advance to avoid surprises and to be able to request appropriate remuneration during interviews.

For those seeking work abroad, international job platforms like Indeed, Monster, Escape the City, and LinkedIn Jobs are indispensable tools. Eures, the European employment service, offers targeted consultations and facilitates the search for employment throughout Europe, while Cinfo is useful for those interested in working for international organizations. These tools can assist Ticino cross-border workers in identifying opportunities that best match their profiles and preparing adequately for the transfer. ### Practical Implications for Ticino Cross-Border Workers

For cross-border workers already employed in Switzerland but looking to explore opportunities abroad, there are several practical considerations to keep in mind. First, the freedom of movement within the EU/EFTA represents a significant advantage. Those holding a G or B permit in Switzerland can easily move to an EU country without facing lengthy bureaucratic procedures. However, it is important to check for any regulatory updates, especially following political changes or bilateral agreements between Switzerland and the EU. For example, the new tax agreement between Switzerland and Italy, which came into force in 2024, introduced some changes in the taxation of cross-border workers, which could influence the decision to move.

Another aspect to consider is the compatibility of social insurance schemes. In Switzerland, cross-border workers are subject to specific regimes for AHV, BVG, and LAMal. When moving abroad, it is necessary to find out how these contributions will be managed in the new country. For example, those moving to Italy may have to deal with a different social security system, with implications for pensions and health insurance. Consultation with Soliswiss or other specialized entities can be useful to avoid problems of double taxation or loss of contributions.

### Country Comparison: Opportunities and Challenges

Not all countries offer the same opportunities for foreign workers. For example, in Germany and France, the official languages (German and French) are often required for many positions, while in countries like Ireland or the Netherlands, English may be sufficient. For Ticino cross-border workers, who often speak Italian, German, and French, opportunities can vary significantly. Here is a comparative table summarizing some of the main differences between EU and non-EU countries:

| **Country** | Main Language | Work Permit | Cost of Living | Protection Against Dismissal |
|------------------|-----------------------|------------------------------|----------------------|-----------------------------|
| Italy | Italian | EU Freedom of Movement | Medium | Medium |
| Germany | German | EU Freedom of Movement | High | High |
| France | French | EU Freedom of Movement | High | High |
| USA | English | Special Visa (e.g., H-1B) | Very High | Low |
| Canada | English/French | Special Visa (e.g., Express Entry) | High | Medium |
| Australia | English | Special Visa (e.g., Skilled Visa) | High | Medium |

This table highlights how working conditions and the cost of living can influence the choice of destination country. For example, while in Italy and Germany cross-border workers can benefit from greater protection against dismissals, in countries like the USA this protection is less guaranteed. Additionally, the cost of living in cities like New York or Sydney can be significantly higher compared to European cities like Milan or Munich.

### Concrete Scenarios: What to Do Before Departure

Before moving, it is essential to prepare adequately. Here are some key steps:

1. Verify permits: Ensure you have all the necessary documents to enter and work in the destination country. For EU countries, freedom of movement simplifies things, but for non-EU countries, you may need to obtain a work visa.

2. Analyze the job market: Identify growing sectors and the most in-demand skills in the country of interest. For example, in Germany, the engineering and IT sectors are particularly dynamic, while in France, the healthcare sector offers many opportunities.

3. Language preparation: Even if English is often sufficient, knowing the local language can make a difference. For Ticino cross-border workers, who already speak multiple languages, this can be a competitive advantage.

4. Tax consultation: Find out about the tax implications of the move, especially to avoid problems of double taxation. For example, those moving to Italy may have to deal with different taxation compared to Switzerland.

5. Network of contacts: Build a network of professional contacts in the destination country, using platforms like LinkedIn or attending networking events.

These steps can help Ticino cross-border workers prepare best for a move abroad, minimizing risks and maximizing opportunities.

To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step guide to job hunting abroad

For cross-border workers from Ticino looking to find a job abroad, here’s a detailed guide on how to proceed, based on information provided by SWI swissinfo.ch and the experts consulted.

The first step is to identify the destination country and assess your professional profile. Useful questions to ask yourself include:
- Which languages do I speak fluently?
- In which countries are my skills most in demand?
- Do I have professional or personal contacts in the country of interest?

For example, a cross-border worker who speaks Italian, German, and French might find interesting opportunities in Germany, France, or Belgium, where these languages are often in demand. It’s also helpful to consult websites like Eures or LinkedIn Jobs to identify growing sectors in the destination country.

#### Step 2: Learn about permits and regulations
For EU/EFTA countries, freedom of movement significantly simplifies procedures. However, for non-EU countries, a visa or work permit is required. Embassies and consulates of the countries of interest provide up-to-date information on the necessary requirements. For example:
- **USA**: H-1B visa for skilled workers.
- Canada: Express Entry program for qualified workers.
- Australia: Skilled Independent visa for professionals.

It’s also advisable to contact organizations like Soliswiss, which offer personalized consultations on legal and practical aspects related to emigration.

#### Step 3: Build a network of contacts
As highlighted by Nicole Töpperwien from Soliswiss, often the easiest way to find a job is through direct contacts. Here are some tips for building a network:
- LinkedIn: Create an up-to-date profile and connect with recruiters and professionals in your field of interest.
- Professional associations: Join associations based in the destination country.
- Networking events: Attend job fairs or industry events, both online and offline.

Julia Meir Lawi from Robert Half Schweiz confirms that having the right contacts can make a difference, especially in competitive job markets.

#### Step 4: Prepare your CV and cover letter
Your CV and cover letter must be tailored to the job market of the destination country. For example:
- Format: In some countries, like the USA, a one-page CV is preferred, while in Europe, a longer format is acceptable.
- Language: Translate your CV into the language of the destination country, if necessary.
- Skills: Highlight transferable skills, such as knowledge of multiple languages, which can be an advantage for cross-border workers from Ticino.

#### Step 5: Apply and prepare for interviews
Once you’ve identified job opportunities of interest, it’s time to apply. Platforms like Indeed, Monster, and LinkedIn Jobs are useful for finding job listings. During interviews, it’s important to:
- Learn about working conditions: Ask about hours, holidays, job security, and salaries.
- Prepare for common questions: For example, why you want to work in that country or what your salary expectations are.
- Assess the cost of living: Ensure the offered salary is adequate for the cost of living in the destination country.

#### Step 6: Managing the practical aspects of the move Once a job is secured, it’s time to organize the relocation. Here are some key considerations: - Insurance: Research how to manage AVS, LPP, and LAMal in the new country. For example, moving to Italy may require navigating a different social security system. - Taxation: Check the tax implications of the move, especially to avoid double taxation issues. A tax advisor can be helpful at this stage. - Housing: Look for temporary or permanent accommodation in the destination country. Websites like Immobiliare.it or Idealista can be useful for finding rental or sale properties. ### Useful tools for cross-border commuters To facilitate the job search abroad, here are some helpful tools: - [Salary calculator](nav:calculator): To compare purchasing power between Switzerland and other countries. - [CHF/EUR exchange rate comparator](nav:exchange): To monitor exchange rates and plan expenses. - [LAMal insurance guide](nav:health): To understand how to manage health insurance during the move. - [Job listings platform](nav:jobs): To find job opportunities abroad. ### Conclusion: An opportunity to seize with awareness Working abroad can be a stimulating opportunity for Ticino cross-border workers, but it requires careful preparation. From verifying permits to building a professional network, each step is crucial for a smooth transition. Understanding local regulations, working conditions, and the cost of living is essential to avoid surprises and negotiate appropriate salary requests. For those who want to delve deeper, organizations like Soliswiss and embassies of target countries offer personalized consultations. Additionally, platforms like Eures and LinkedIn Jobs can help identify the most suitable opportunities for one’s profile. With the right preparation, the dream of working abroad can become an accessible and rewarding reality.

## Neutralising estimates: a vote that affects the pockets of cross-border workers

On 14 June 2026, the people of Ticino will be called to the polls to decide on an initiative that, more than others, will directly enter the homes of those who live and work on the border: the initiative "Yes to the neutralisation of the increase in estimated values". Behind this technical term lies a decision that could change the tax pressure, access to social benefits and the quality of life of thousands of cross-border workers. In Ticino, where wages are often low, health insurance premiums are among the highest in Switzerland and the cost of living is among the highest, every small increase in taxes weighs like a millstone. And the tax estimates risk precisely this: making citizens who, in reality, are already struggling at the end of the month appear "richer" on paper.

For those who live and work on the border, between Como, Varese and Ticino, the consequences would be immediate. An increase in estimated values would result in an increase in taxable assets, with a consequent increase in taxes to be paid. For a cross-border worker who owns their own home, this would mean seeing the tax value of the property increase and, consequently, paying more taxes even on the home in which they live. Not only that: exceeding decisive thresholds for access to benefits such as reductions in health insurance premiums, scholarships or other social benefits would become more difficult. Here is the paradox: being "too rich" to receive support, but not rich enough to live without difficulty.

## A tax system that does not correspond to reality

The neutralisation of estimates is not an ideological proposal, but a response to a system that risks moving further and further away from the concrete lives of people. Today, tax estimates consider the home as a source of income, when in reality it is the result of years of sacrifice: a security, a rooting, an investment that does not produce income but is taxed as if it did. For cross-border workers, who have often built their stability with responsibility and sacrifices, this mechanism is particularly unfair. The house, for them, is not a luxury but the result of daily work that crosses the border every morning.

The issue worsens when considering that, in Ticino, salaries are generally low compared to the rest of Switzerland. An increase in wealth taxes or the taxable value of property would particularly affect those who have already struggled to build their future. The risk is fueling an increasingly widespread sense of injustice: why should those who have already paid taxes on their income have to pay more on the value of a home that has already been financed?

Imagine a cross-border worker who owns a house in Chiasso or Stabio, purchased after years of working in Switzerland. Today, the fiscal value of the property is calculated according to parameters that could be updated upwards. If the estimates increase, the taxable value grows, and so do the wealth taxes. For a worker who crosses the border every day, this means seeing their purchasing power eroded without a concrete reason. This is why on June 14, 2026, we are not just voting on a technical mechanism, but on a choice of equity.

- If it passes: The estimates remain unchanged, avoiding increases in property taxes and maintaining access to social benefits for those in need. The tax burden on the middle class is lightened, and the primary residence is not further penalized.
- If it fails: The estimates could increase, leading to a consequent rise in wealth taxes and a reduction in the available taxable income. For cross-border workers who own a home, this would mean paying more on a property that has already been financed with previously taxed income.

> *The neutralization of the estimates goes in the opposite direction, to restore balance, avoid distortions, and prevent a theoretical value from becoming an additional tax burden.*

Even those who work in Ticino but live in Italy could be affected by this decision. If the estimates increase, property taxes in Ticino could rise, indirectly affecting disposable income. Furthermore, the reduction in access to social benefits in Ticino could have repercussions on family members living across the border. In Ticino, the middle class is increasingly squeezed between two extremes. On one side, low salaries compared to the rest of Switzerland and high health insurance premiums. It relies on the collaboration between 25 member states, ten associate member states, and observers such as the United States and the European Union. But it also relies on the premise that some questions are too big to find answers in the efforts of a single country. Questions like: What is the universe made of? Why does matter exist? What happened in the instants just after the Big Bang?

CERN's premise has borne fruit in 2012 when scientists working at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) announced the discovery of the Higgs boson. The so-called God Particle gives mass to fundamental particles, the smallest building blocks of the universe. 'Without the Higgs boson, we wouldn't be here,' explains Fabiola Gianotti, who was the director-general of CERN for ten years until January of this year.

That discovery, however, has raised as many questions as it has answered. And now, as LHC is reaching the limit of what it can reveal, CERN has its most audacious move yet: a new particle accelerator, almost four times larger than LHC, placed 200 meters deep and destined to pass under Lake Geneva and the Rhône River. item.description: Practical tips to prepare a convincing application dossier for working abroad.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief
- Preparation of the curriculum vitae and application dossier for abroad.
- Cultural sensitivity and language requirements.
- Specific advice for USA, Canada, France, Germany, and Asia.

## Key Facts
- **What**: Preparation of the curriculum vitae and application dossier for abroad.
- When: Always necessary for those applying abroad.
- Where: Worldwide, with cultural variations.
- Who: Candidates seeking employment abroad.
- Amount: Not specified.

When applying for a job abroad, it's not enough to just adapt linguistically; cultural sensitivity is also necessary. What is normal in Switzerland may be completely different in other countries like the USA, France, or Japan.

### General Advice
Specify diplomas and their equivalent titles so that potential employers can get a clear idea of various skills. Indicate the type of residence and work permit; do not lie about language skills: native speakers would notice immediately. Do not forget to indicate the correct phone prefix and perhaps the time zone as well.

In Switzerland, it is normal to include in the curriculum vitae, with a photo, the date of birth and marital status. Elsewhere, this practice is not always common, so in case of doubt, it is better to omit such information. Update your application dossier so that it meets the requirements of the country you will move to. Employment offices abroad can provide a more in-depth overview of the local job market, trends in various sectors, and cultural nuances.

### Country-Specific Advice
Often in the USA and Canada, application dossiers are more sober compared to what we are used to in Switzerland. Most of the time, a curriculum vitae and a brief cover letter are sufficient. 'The curriculum vitae is usually sent without a photo; often, employers prefer this solution due to anti-discrimination laws,' says Julia Meir Lawi, Branch Director Geneva at the recruitment company Robert Half Schweiz.

Personal information such as date of birth, marital status, or religion should not be included. However, in the USA and Canada, job interviews are often more informal and personal. 'The so-called cultural fit is fundamental: one must demonstrate a certain affinity with the company.' In the USA, salary negotiation is generally expected and considered a normal part of the hiring process. Moreover, as Anthony Adam of Page Executive, a recruitment company, states, 'In the USA, security checks on the individual, including criminal record checks, are common in many sectors.'

In some European countries like France and Germany, salary structures are more rigid, and often a photo cannot be missing from the application dossier. These are the words of Julia Meir Lawi of Robert Half Schweiz: 'The process for finding a job in France is characterized by formal schemes, which require the job interview to be equally formal.' The same goes for Germany, where it is not uncommon – always according to Julia Meir Lawi – for technical skills to be tested and a focus on professional compatibility.

In Asia, the weight of hierarchies is often much more marked; the application processes are intensive, relatively long, and complex. Modesty and the ability to work within a team are required. According to Julia Meir Lawi, in Japan, companies expect a high degree of formality; application dossiers must be strongly focused on the company and its philosophy. Since the crucial element is the team, it is rare during the job interview for personal questions to be asked. ### Practical Implications for Cross-Border Workers
For cross-border workers wishing to work abroad, it is essential to adapt your curriculum vitae (CV) and application portfolio to the specific requirements of the destination country. This includes translating diplomas and certifications, as well as updating personal and professional information.

### Country Comparison
In the USA and Canada, application portfolios are generally more understated and less formal than those required in Switzerland. In France and Germany, however, it is common to include a photograph in your CV and to follow formal structures during the selection process. In Asia, especially in Japan, application processes are longer and more complex, with a greater emphasis on formality and compatibility with the company's philosophy.

### Concrete Scenarios
A cross-border worker applying for a job in the USA should prepare a CV without a photo and a brief cover letter. During the interview, it will be important to demonstrate a certain affinity with the company and to prepare to negotiate salary. In France, on the other hand, the process will be more formal, with a greater emphasis on technical skills and professional compatibility.

### Concrete Procedures
To prepare a compelling application portfolio, it is important to follow these steps:
1. Translate diplomas and certifications.
2. Indicate the type of residence and work permit (e.g., G permit).
3. Do not lie about language skills.
4. Indicate the correct country code and time zone.
5. Omit personal information such as date of birth and marital status, unless requested.
6. Update your application portfolio according to the requirements of the destination country.
7. Consult foreign employment offices to gain a more in-depth overview of the local job market.

item.title: Cost of Living in Switzerland 2026: Cantons
item.description: How much does it cost to live in Switzerland in 2026? A canton-by-canton comparison of rent, health premiums, taxes and daily spending.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Living in Switzerland in 2026 costs on average between CHF 4,000 and 6,500 a month for a single person, depending on the canton
- Zug, Zurich and Geneva remain the most expensive cantons; Jura, Valais and Appenzell are among the most affordable
- Rent and health-insurance premiums account for over 40% of a household budget

## Key facts
- **Average rent (4 rooms)**: from CHF 1,300 in Jura to over CHF 2,700 in Zurich and Geneva
- 2026 adult health premium: national average CHF 393/month, +6% on 2025
- Tax burden: in Zug an income of CHF 100,000 pays around 7% in cantonal and communal tax, in Geneva it can exceed 18%
- Groceries: roughly CHF 400-600 per month per person
- Public transport: a 2nd-class GA travelcard costs CHF 3,995/year

Living in Switzerland means dealing with one of the highest costs of living in Europe, but also with some of the best salaries and public services in the world. In 2026 the gap between cantons remains wide: the same household can spend 40-50% more in Geneva than in Jura on rent, taxes and insurance. Understanding where and how money is spent is the first step to planning a move or simply balancing the budget.

### Rent: the biggest single expense

Rent is the largest single outlay for most Swiss households. In 2026 a four-room apartment costs on average around CHF 1,300 a month in rural cantons such as Jura or Neuchâtel, but easily exceeds CHF 2,700 in the urban areas of Zurich, Zug and Geneva. In Lugano and Bellinzona prices are intermediate, around CHF 1,700-2,000. Pressure on rents stays high in cities because of low vacancy rates, often below 1%.

### Taxes: the factor that reshuffles the ranking

The tax burden changes dramatically from canton to canton and from municipality to municipality. Zug, Schwyz and Nidwalden offer some of the lowest rates in the Confederation, which is why they attract high incomes and companies. At the opposite end, Geneva, Vaud and Bern apply steeper progression. For a taxable income of CHF 100,000, the annual tax difference between the cheapest and the most expensive municipality can exceed CHF 10,000.

### Health insurance and daily spending

Mandatory health-insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG) rise by an average of 6% in 2026 and vary considerably by canton: Basel-City, Geneva and Ticino stay above the national average, while Appenzell Innerrhoden and Uri are among the cheapest. Add to this groceries (CHF 400-600 per person per month), rising electricity costs and transport. The strong franc makes imported goods expensive but benefits those who shop across the border. ### What it means for those living in or moving to Switzerland

Choosing the canton and municipality of residence is a long-term financial decision. Two households with the same gross income can end up with very different purchasing power depending on where they live: the combination of rent, communal tax rate and health premium can be worth several thousand francs a year. Before signing a lease it is therefore worth simulating the full budget, not just comparing the rent.

### Salary and real purchasing power

A high salary alone is not enough: what matters is the net amount left after taxes, insurance premiums and housing costs. In low-tax cantons such as Zug or Schwyz, even higher rents can be offset by tax savings. To orient yourself, compare your expected net salary with the [cost of living per canton](nav:cost-of-living) and check how much health insurance really weighs on your monthly budget in the [health insurance](nav:health) section.

### The role of the exchange rate and cross-border shopping

Those living near the border, especially in Ticino, Basel or Geneva, can cut some costs by buying groceries and fuel in neighbouring countries. The strong franc amplifies this advantage, but customs allowances and travel time must be taken into account. To manage currency exchanges efficiently, keep an eye on the [CHF-EUR rate](nav:exchange). ### How to optimise your cost of living in Switzerland

Here are some concrete steps to keep spending under control, whatever canton you live in:

1. **Compare municipalities, not just cantons**: within the same canton the communal tax multiplier can vary significantly. Use cantonal tax calculators before choosing where to live.
2. **Review your health insurance every year**: switching insurer or raising your deductible before the end of November can save several hundred francs a year.
3. **Pick the right transport pass**: for commuters the GA travelcard pays off beyond a certain distance; below that, point-to-point passes are cheaper.
4. **Plan housing ahead**: in cities with vacancy below 1% it pays to apply early and widen the search to neighbouring municipalities, which are often cheaper.
5. **Use tax deductions**: pillar 3a, professional expenses and insurance premiums reduce taxable income.

### In conclusion

The cost of living in Switzerland in 2026 remains high but extremely variable from canton to canton. Rent, taxes and health premiums are the three main levers to act on: a deliberate choice of where to live and an annual review of your insurance can make the difference between a stretched budget and solid saving capacity. Always compare the real net amount, not just the gross, before making important decisions.

item.title: Health Premiums 2026: What Changes Switzerland
item.description: Mandatory LAMal health-insurance premiums rise by about 6% on average in 2026. Cantonal differences, deductibles and how to save.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Mandatory health-insurance premiums (LAMal) rise by an average of 6% across Switzerland in 2026
- The average monthly adult premium climbs to about CHF 393, up from CHF 371 in 2025
- The increase hits every canton, but with sharp differences between Appenzell Innerrhoden and Geneva

## Key facts
- **Average adult premium 2026**: CHF 393/month (national average)
- Average increase: about +6% on 2025
- Average young-adult premium (19-25): around CHF 277/month
- Average child premium: around CHF 100/month
- Minimum adult deductible: CHF 300; maximum CHF 2,500
- Individual premium reduction (IPR): cantonal subsidy for low-to-middle incomes

In 2026 mandatory health-insurance premiums rise again across Switzerland. According to the Federal Office of Public Health, the average monthly premium for an adult climbs to about CHF 393, an average increase of 6% on the previous year. It is the third consecutive year of significant rises, driven by growing healthcare costs, an ageing population and more reimbursed treatments.

### Why premiums keep rising

The increase reflects the structural growth of health costs: more medical visits, more medication, more hospital stays and costly new therapies. Added to this is the rebuilding of insurers' reserves, partly eroded in recent years. The premium does not depend on income but on the canton, the premium region, age and the chosen insurance model. That is why two people with the same income can pay very different amounts.

### Differences between cantons

Cantonal disparities remain considerable. Geneva, Basel-City, Vaud and Ticino are among the cantons with the highest premiums, while Appenzell Innerrhoden, Uri, Nidwalden and Obwalden remain the cheapest. The difference between the most expensive and the cheapest canton can exceed CHF 150 a month for an adult, that is over CHF 1,800 a year. Within the same canton there are also several premium regions.

### What changes for families

For a family with two adults and two children, the 6% rise can mean several hundred francs more per year. Households on a low-to-middle income, however, can apply for the individual premium reduction (IPR), a cantonal subsidy that eases the burden. The income thresholds and amounts vary from canton to canton, but the application must be filed every year with the competent cantonal authority. ### What it means for people living in Switzerland

The 2026 premium increase directly affects every household budget. Because the premium is independent of income, it weighs proportionally more on lower-income families. It is therefore essential to review your cover every year: insurance model, deductible and insurer can all be changed before the end-of-November cancellation deadline. A careful comparison can offset much of the rise.

### How to choose your deductible and model

The annual deductible ranges from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500: a high deductible lowers the monthly premium but exposes you to higher costs if you fall ill. Those in good health who rarely use medical services can save with a high deductible; those with recurring treatment are often better off on the minimum. Alternative models (family doctor, HMO, telemedicine) offer premium discounts in exchange for a defined care pathway. To estimate the impact on your budget, use the [health insurance](nav:health) section and compare scenarios with the [calculator](nav:calculator).

### Premiums and the overall cost of living

Health insurance is, together with rent, one of the two heaviest items in a Swiss budget. It is therefore worth assessing it in the context of the [cost of living per canton](nav:cost-of-living): in some cases a higher premium is offset by lower taxes, in others not. An overall view helps you understand where it really pays to live. ### What to do before the end-of-November deadline

Here are the concrete steps to deal with the 2026 premium increase:

1. **Compare insurers**: use the official comparison tool priminfo.admin.ch to see all premiums for your canton and region. For the same basic cover, differences between insurers can exceed CHF 100 a month.
2. Reassess your deductible: if you had few medical expenses last year, consider raising it to lower the premium.
3. Consider an alternative model: family doctor, HMO or telemedicine offer discounts often above 10%.
4. Check your right to a premium reduction: review your canton's income thresholds and file the IPR application if you qualify.
5. Cancel in time: the cancellation of basic insurance must be sent by 30 November to take effect on 1 January.

### In conclusion

In 2026 health-insurance premiums rise by an average of 6% across Switzerland, but those who act in time can limit the impact. Comparing insurers, choosing the right deductible, considering an alternative model and applying for the cantonal subsidy when entitled are the main levers. An annual review, done before the end of November, is the most effective way to keep this mandatory expense under control.

*Fonte: [Ufficio federale della sanità pubblica](https://www.bag.admin.ch/bag/it/home/versicherungen/krankenversicherung/krankenversicherung-praemien.html)*
